title: Changing Your Mind
objective: After this level you can update a belief in proportion to new evidence, rather than all at once or not at all.
summary: Belief comes in degrees. Hume's rule, proportion your belief to the evidence, plus open-mindedness: suspend judgment when evidence is thin, take a position when it is enough.

cards.headline: New evidence arrives. Do you flip, dig in, or shift a little?
cards.body: Say you've always heard a bakery makes the best croissants in town, and a friend tells you hers was stale. Throwing out your belief would be too much. Ignoring your friend would be too little. This level is about the space in between.

cards.headline: Belief comes in degrees
cards.body: In his 1748 Enquiry, the philosopher David Hume noticed that when we reason about matters of fact, there are all degrees of assurance, from the highest certainty down to the weakest evidence. Belief isn't an on-off switch. It works more like a dial, and the evidence should set how far it turns.

cards.headline: Proportion your belief
cards.body: Hume's rule follows. When evidence points both ways, weigh the opposing cases, lean toward the side with more support, and hold that view with doubt and hesitation. One stale croissant nudges the dial. A dozen friends with stale croissants should turn it a long way.
cards.callout: Hume: "A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence."

cards.headline: Open, not empty
cards.body: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy counts open-mindedness among a critical thinker's habits: being willing to re-examine a question you've already answered, if further evidence or reasoning might change your answer. Its partner habit is suspending judgment when the evidence is insufficient and taking a position once it's enough. Changing your mind, in proportion, is the point.

cards.headline: Beliefs: updated in proportion
learned: Belief comes in degrees, from certainty to weak evidence
Hume: proportion your belief to the evidence
Small evidence moves a belief a little; strong evidence, a lot
Suspend judgment when evidence is thin; decide when it is enough

questions.prompt: What was David Hume's rule for how strongly to believe something?

options.label: Believe what most people around you believe
options.rationale: Popularity is not the measure Hume gave.

options.label: Never believe anything without certainty
options.rationale: Hume allowed every degree of assurance, not only certainty.

options.label: Proportion your belief to the evidence
Keep a belief once you have formed it
options.rationale: Hume expected belief to follow the evidence.

questions.explanation: A wise man, Hume wrote, proportions his belief to the evidence.

questions.prompt: Match each response to the croissant news with its description.

pairs.left: A dozen friends with stale croissants

questions.explanation: Throwing out your belief would be too much, and ignoring your friend too little. One stale croissant nudges the dial; a dozen friends with stale croissants should turn it a long way.

questions.prompt: Dewey called suspended judgment the essence of critical thinking. According to the Stanford Encyclopedia, judgment should be suspended _____.

options.label: whenever a question matters
options.rationale: Importance is not the test; the evidence is.

options.label: until everyone involved agrees
options.rationale: Agreement is not the test either.

options.label: forever, on every question
options.rationale: Once the evidence is enough, you take a position.

questions.explanation: Seeking the truth means suspending judgment when the evidence is insufficient and adopting a position when it is sufficient.
